summary:
Sort the scores once. In sorted order, the scores within `[lo, hi]` are one contiguous block, from the first
score ≥ lo to just before the first score > hi. Two binary searches per query give its size: O((n + q) log n).

question.md:
For each query `[lo, hi]`, count the scores with `lo ≤ score ≤ hi`, answering in order.

- **The scores are unsorted**, but we may sort a copy: queries only ask how many, not which ones.
- **Inclusive bounds**, and repeated scores each count.
- **Many queries:** up to 10⁵ queries over 10⁵ scores, so scanning all scores per query (10¹⁰) is too slow.

think.md:
Take `scores = [70, 85, 90, 60, 85, 72, 99, 55]`. Sorted: `[55, 60, 70, 72, 85, 85, 90, 99]`. For the query [70, 86], the qualifying scores 70, 72, 85, 85 sit
next to each other in sorted order.

think.caption: Scores within a range are always one block of the sorted list.

think.md:
The block starts at the **lower bound** of lo (first score ≥ lo) and ends just before the **upper bound** of
hi (first score > hi). Their difference is the count. Sorting costs O(n log n) once; each query then costs
two O(log n) searches.

approaches.title: Scan all scores per query

idea.md: For each query, count the scores between lo and hi with a full pass.

build: For each query, loop over all scores and count those with `lo ≤ s ≤ hi`.

complexity.md: **Time O(n · q).** **Space O(1)** besides the output.

walk.title: For every query, scan all scores and count those inside the range.

limits.md: Every query re-reads every score. Sorting once makes each query's matches a block whose ends can be binary-searched.

approaches.title: Sort once, two binary searches per query

idea.md: Sort a copy. For each query: `a` = first index with score ≥ lo, `b` = first index with score > hi. Answer `b − a`.

build: Sort a copy of the scores.
For each query, compute the lower bound of lo and the upper bound of hi.

lines.text: `firstAbove(x)` is the upper bound: the first index whose value exceeds x. "First ≥ lo" equals "first > lo − 1" for integers, so one helper serves both ends; `lo − 1` is computed in 64 bits because lo can be −10⁹.
Scores in `[lo, hi]` are the block from the first value ≥ lo up to (not including) the first value > hi.

notes.python: `bisect_left` is the lower bound, `bisect_right` the upper bound.
notes.cpp: `lower_bound(lo)` and `upper_bound(hi)` bracket exactly the scores in range.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n + q log n).** **Space O(n)** for the sorted copy.

steps.text: Query [70, 86]: first ≥ 70 is index 2; first > 86 is index 6; count 6 − 2 = 4.
Query [0, 59]: first ≥ 0 is index 0; first > 59 is index 1; count 1 − 0 = 1.
Query [85, 85]: first ≥ 85 is index 4; first > 85 is index 6; count 6 − 4 = 2.

walk.title: Sort once. For each query, the matching scores form one block: [first ≥ lo, first > hi).

takeaways.md:
- **Count in [lo, hi] on sorted data** = `upperBound(hi) − lowerBound(lo)`.
- Sorting once pays off when many queries follow.
- For integers, "≥ lo" equals "> lo − 1", so one bound function can serve both ends.
